newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Brown wins over markets at a stroke.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Brown wins over markets at a stroke.

text.p: Britain's financial markets have become less worried by the prospect of a Labour government in recent years but Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown turned cautious optimism to instant idolatry at a stroke on Tuesday.

Brown raised interest rates after only four days in government -- a long overdue move as far as many were concerned -- but he really stunned the markets by also making the Bank of England effectively independent.
In one decisive move, he has won his spurs with the City.
"What one thought would be a reasonably routine announcement on interest rates, became astonishing," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

Brown will set up a nine-member monetary policy committee to oversee monetary policy. The Treasury will retain control of the inflation target -- currently 2.5 percent or less -- but will not have a vote on the committee, leaving the Bank free to set interest rates to meet the inflation goal.
"It's incredibly bold and a welcome step," Shepperd said.
By giving the Bank its head over interest rates, Brown has largely removed the threat of monetary policy being prey to political manipulation.
As a result, investors can be more confident inflation -- the markets' bete noire -- will remain nailed down in Britain.

Market reaction was little short of supersonic. The long gilt future rocketed by more than 2-1/2 points in less than an hour. Not since John Major's Conservatives secured a shock election win in 1992 have government bonds risen more in one session.
The FTSE 100 index of leading UK shares followed suit, jumping nearly 70 points to 4,525. And the pound leaped nearly three pfennigs against the mark.
"It smacks of seriousness, conviction, decisiveness. The markets have loved it," one trader said. "It wipes the floor with previous Chancellors."

Kenneth Clarke, Brown's predecessor, won the respect of the traditionally Tory-supporting markets by delivering a sustained period of low inflation, low interest rates and steady economic growth. But dealers say Brown has topped him in one swoop.
"We might have got all this cynicism about the Labour Party seriously wrong," the trader said.

Labour spent the last five years in opposition carefully wooing business leaders and City high flyers. First there was former Labour leader John Smith's so-called "prawn cocktail" offensive, a series of informal business lunches.
Alastair Darling, now Brown's number two at the Treasury, carried on the good work and Labour's Business Relations Unit, run by Geoff Hoon, even gained the support of several top businessmen.
Brown has not only surpassed their efforts but taken Labour's standing in the City a giant leap forward.

By acting so quickly, he has portrayed himself as a dynamic Chancellor and also neatly sidestepped the risk of looking like he fell to Bank of England Governor Eddie George's demands for higher rates at the first fence. George has demanded a rate rise throughout this year.
For the first time in living memory, an interest rate rise has taken a back seat to other events as far as the markets are concerned.

Almost incidentally, base rates were raised by a quarter-point to 6.25 percent. Of course, Brown could still use the fiscal side of the policy equation to return to the bad old days of a high spending, high taxation Labour government. But nobody expects him to and even if he did, Tuesday's reforms would allow the Bank of England freedom to redress the balance anyway.
"The government still has control of fiscal policy but any irresponsibility there would swiftly be countered by the newly freed Bank," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.
